data.title: Building campaign action pages on Cloudflare
data.summary: Notes on an unfinished campaign-software experiment: forms, storage, and integrations on Cloudflare Workers.

children.text: Campaign forms often need the same pieces: a page editor, submission storage, exports, confirmation messages, and connections to other tools. I explored putting those pieces in an EmDash plugin called Action Pages. The project remains unfinished; these notes describe the implementation so far.
Rendering and storage

Astro renders the page around a React form. EmDash stores the content and configuration, and Cloudflare Workers handles requests. D1 stores submissions, KV holds counters and cached data, and R2 stores uploaded media. The plugin provides templates and an editor for configuring pages without changing the site’s source code.
Handling a submission

The submission route validates the request, applies rate limits and geographic filters, checks for duplicate email addresses, and writes accepted records to D1. Turnstile verification is an external request when a token and secret are present; the current route does not require a token for every page.

After the database write, the Worker schedules the notification and integration work with waitUntil. This includes confirmation email, campaign-platform updates, and contact records. A successful form response means the submission was stored; it does not guarantee that every downstream service accepted its update.

Keeping that work out of the response path avoids making the form wait for every integration. It also leaves an operational problem worth handling explicitly: failures after a submission is accepted need monitoring and a retry strategy.
Trying it
The
project page
links to example forms and the embed generator. The
source
contains the plugin;
this site’s repository
shows how it is integrated.
Hosting costs depend on traffic, storage, email, and the services configured for a deployment.

data.title: CharterCostTracker
data.summary: A Python system for estimating charter transfers’ effects on district revenue, covering 1,023 Texas districts over five years.

children.text: I built CharterCostTracker to collect Texas education data, estimate how charter transfers affect district revenue, and generate reports for Texas AFT and public education advocates. I handled all the programming and engineering, expanding a manual district-by-district process into a five-year dataset covering 1,023 districts.

The project began with constituent concerns about a proposed charter campus while I was a legislative director. A longtime advocate and mentor had developed an estimation method and statement-of-impact template with school finance experts. I translated that method into code and reviewed the calculations with her as we expanded the analysis statewide.
Data and calculations

I collected TEA directory, enrollment, transfer, finance, accountability, and recapture records. Selenium scripts located reports in TEA’s interactive report builder; an asynchronous downloader retrieved them with retries and checks for missing or incomplete files. I retained source URLs, report dates, run IDs, and payment cycles.

The parsers handle changing spreadsheet layouts, restore leading zeros in district IDs, and reconcile district and charter names. The calculations combine transfer counts with funding, attendance, and enrollment data, accounting for changes in formulas and report formats across years.

The reports keep observed transfers separate from estimates for masked counts. One later scenario assumes five transfers per receiving charter entity with a masked count and reports that estimate separately.
Reports and publication
I automated statewide spreadsheets, district breakdowns, Word and PDF reports, maps, and charts. I also generated responsive HTML tables linking to district reports for Texas AFT’s website.
I wrote the entire June 27, 2024 Texas AFT article,
“The Growing Financial Strain of Charter School Expansion on Texas Public Schools”
, presenting the findings and their implications. The link opens an archived copy because the original URL is no longer available.

I continue to prepare analyses for hearings, town halls, and discussions about school closures and budget cuts. This work also supported research for Our Schools, Our Democracy and informed the data-collection tools in

data.title: HB 2 Support-Staff Raise Analysis
data.summary: Statewide funding models and local organizing materials to help Texas AFT explain what HB 2 could mean for school support staff.

children.text: After Texas passed HB 2 in 2025, I modeled the funding available for support-staff raises across 1,179 school systems. I did this work for Texas AFT through Data for Public Education.

I checked the allocation formulas, matched staffing records, and documented fallback rules where a district’s data was missing or inconsistent. The deliverables included statewide analyses, audit workbooks, one-pagers, and 35 customized PDFs for local leaders. I also corrected graphics and reports as the review progressed.

The public workbook below examines the Support Staff Retention Allotment, including how adjusted attendance affects the allocation. It is one part of the project. Its paraprofessional staffing counts differ from the broader support-staff counts used for the newsletter’s raise examples.
These are estimates under stated assumptions. A funding allocation is not a guarantee that an employee received a particular raise.

data.title: SB 9 Teacher Pay Analysis
data.summary: District-level estimates of the costs and effects of teacher-pay proposals in the 2023 Texas legislative session.

children.text: I analyzed SB 9 and related teacher-retention proposals during the 2023 Texas legislative session. The question was how each funding design would affect districts and what it would cost statewide.

I joined district directory records with staffing and full-time-equivalent data, calculated the scenarios, and exported workbooks for review. I also mapped the share of teachers with six or more years of experience using district boundaries and staffing records.

children.text: I built this pipeline to examine the Texas Education Freedom Account school-finder data outside its search interface. It collects the Comptroller’s vendor feed and supporting metadata, normalizes the records, and adds county, school-district, and education-service-center geography.

The outputs include vendor-level CSVs and an Excel workbook with filterable tables for services, specialties, and vendor types. Cached source files and geographic inputs document how the records were collected and joined.

data.title: The Lost Decade (and a Half)
data.summary: Texas educator-pay research: I wrote the 2024 report, performed all the analysis, and built its responsive web tables.

children.text: I wrote all of Texas AFT’s 2024 report, The Lost Decade (and a Half), and performed all of its analysis. I also created the responsive HTML tables for the website, which connected readers to their districts’ results.

The report followed educator pay over time and adjusted it for inflation. It found that average Texas teacher pay had lost more than 9% of its purchasing power between the 2009–2010 and 2023–2024 school years. The district analyses showed how much that experience varied across the state.
I built the salary datasets, district analyses, spreadsheets, and web tables so readers could check the local figures behind the statewide findings. The related
Respect Campaign Map
gave educators and organizers another way to find district research.

data.title: comma.ai Video Compression Challenge
data.summary: Ongoing video-compression research, with three submissions that have appeared on comma.ai’s leaderboard.

children.text: I’m working on comma.ai’s lossy video compression challenge: making a driving video smaller while preserving what the challenge’s segmentation and motion-estimation models see. That means testing both the file size and the effect of compression on those models.
I use
comma-lab
for experiments, decoders, evaluation tools, and research records.
tac
contains reusable training, compression, and validation code. I develop across Apple Silicon and Linux GPU environments and check submission archives with the challenge’s evaluator.
Leaderboard submissions
My submissions
, and
have all appeared on the
official leaderboard
#107, Apogee: an HNeRV-based representation with a deterministic decoder.
#110: per-frame-pair corrections selected against both segmentation and pose distortion, stored with fixed Huffman coding.
#140: semantic edits and pose compensation, combined with improvements to lossless coding and the archive format.

These submissions build on credited public work. #110 uses #101’s HNeRV representation; #140 builds on the learned renderer and pose components in #130 and #135, including #133’s contributions. The pull requests describe my optimization, selection, coding, and validation work.
For a more visual introduction to related research,
The Witness Machine
is an interactive notebook about allocating compression error around what a perception model needs. Its demonstrations are separate from official challenge scores.
The research is ongoing. These leaderboard results apply to the challenge’s fixed video and evaluators.

data.title: Molt
data.summary: A compiler for turning a supported subset of Python into standalone native binaries and WebAssembly.

children.text: I’m building Molt to ship Python applications without requiring a Python installation on the machine that runs them. The compiler targets CPython 3.12+ behavior for the subset of the language it supports.

Molt analyzes the whole program, infers types, and removes unused code before generating a binary. The backend is written in Rust. Native compilation and WebAssembly have separate output paths, and differential tests compare supported behavior with CPython.

The project is still in development. Compatibility varies by application and target; WebAssembly parity is incomplete. Unrestricted runtime code execution and monkeypatching are outside the compiled-language design. The
current status
and
getting-started guide
cover what works and how to try it.

The example on this page runs a Python Mandelbrot program that I compiled with Molt. It executes WebAssembly in your browser and shows the program’s standard output. The Python source, compiled binary, and build record are available alongside it.

data.title: Notifications
data.summary: A TypeScript library for sending one message through multiple services and reporting what succeeded, failed, or was skipped.

children.text: I built Notifications to keep delivery code out of the rest of an application. A caller supplies one message; adapters handle the details for email, chat, and other services.

Configured adapters run in parallel, each with its own timeout. A failed service does not prevent the others from finishing, and the caller gets a result listing deliveries, failures, and skipped channels.
The demo runs the actual dispatcher with local mock adapters. Try making one channel fail or time out while another succeeds. It does not send messages or require credentials.

data.title: Reproq
data.summary: Background tasks for Django and PostgreSQL, with a Go worker and a terminal dashboard.

children.text: I built Reproq for Django applications that already use PostgreSQL and need background jobs. The
Django package
handles task definitions, scheduling, and results. A separate
Go worker
claims and executes jobs.

Workers use PostgreSQL’s SKIP LOCKED mechanism to claim available tasks. The system supports delayed and periodic jobs, priorities, deduplication, and concurrency limits. Management commands cover cancellation, logs, configuration checks, and worker upgrades.
I also built
Reproq TUI
, a terminal dashboard for queue depth, throughput, failures, and worker health. It connects to worker metrics and can include Django-side statistics.
Reproq is in alpha. The setup guide documents deployment requirements, including running one scheduler per database.

data.title: Texas Inflation Calculator
data.summary: A browser calculator for comparing purchasing power across years using CPI data published by the Texas Comptroller.

children.text: Enter a dollar amount and choose two periods to see how its purchasing power changes after inflation. I built the calculator as a static page with Vue, Papa Parse, and Chart.js; the chart shows the CPI values used in the calculation.
The
source repository

includes the page and a CSV from the Texas Comptroller’s Key Economic Indicators dataset. Results use that saved data release, so the available periods depend on when the CSV was last updated. The app needs no server or build step.

data.title: Travis County Voter Data
data.summary: A voter-data application for searching registration and election history, mapping records, and building lists.

children.text: I built a database and web application around Travis County’s public voter-registration and election-history files. Campaign researchers could search records, inspect voting history, build lists, draw organizing areas on a map, and export CSVs.

My work covered file ingestion, geocoding, record matching, and the search interface. I used Python, Go, Flask, PostgreSQL, and SQLite across the project, including SQLAlchemy filters and handwritten SQL for similarity ranking. I also replaced hardcoded election rules with mappings that could accommodate new county files.
This is a historical project; the portfolio does not expose voter records or a live search service.
